blocks.text: **Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO)** is impaired venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs through the SVC. It happens in two broad ways: **extrinsic** — a mass outside the vessel presses on (or invades) the vein; or **intraluminal** — the lumen is blocked from within, usually by thrombus (for example around a central venous catheter, or tumour-related thromboembolism).

blocks.title: Where it sits in acute oncology
items: Davidson groups SVCO with the **emergency complications of cancer**, together with spinal cord compression, hypercalcaemia and neutropenic fever.
In Kumar & Clark’s acute oncology table, a **swollen face** in a patient with cancer points first to SVCO.
Zero to Finals calls it a **medical emergency** and a complication of lung cancer, from the tumour pressing directly on the SVC.

Other emergencies in the same lists: **tumour lysis syndrome** after treatment (high urate, potassium and phosphate, low calcium), **cord compression** (new leg weakness; whole-spine MRI) and **neutropenic fever** (Davidson: 38°C for over an hour with neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L).

blocks.text: Severity depends on a race between **how fast the SVC closes** and **how well venous collaterals open up**. Sudden occlusion gives dramatic swelling; slow occlusion lets collaterals form over weeks, so symptoms build gradually.

blocks.title: Causes of SVCO by mechanism
rows: Lung cancer is the commonest cause, usually through malignant mediastinal lymph nodes pressing on the SVC
Leukaemia (mediastinal mass is typical of ALL), malignant thymic tumours, germ-cell tumours, mesothelioma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma can also cause other compression syndromes (gut obstruction, cord compression)
Large retrosternal goitre; thoracic aortic or innominate aneurysm; benign mediastinal tumours and cysts
Benign masses seldom invade but can still squeeze the SVC or trachea
Central venous catheter thrombosis; tumour-associated thromboembolism
Line-related subclavian thrombosis is often seen on imaging, but clinical SVC syndrome from it is rare

blocks.title: Lung cancer and SVCO
items: Kumar: any upper mediastinal mass can obstruct the SVC, but **lung cancer and lymphoma** are the usual culprits.
Step-Up quotes SVC syndrome in about **5% of lung cancer** patients, more often with **small-cell** disease, although NSCLC can do it too.
Mechanism: a centrally placed tumour, or its involved nodes, compresses the vein.

blocks.note: Look at: a bulky anterior mediastinal mass (T-lymphoblastic lymphoma) in a patient who presented with SVCO.

blocks.text: Mediastinal mass plus SVCO: think beyond lung cancer nodes to **lymphoma** (including T-lymphoblastic), **ALL**, **thymic** and **germ-cell tumours**. Histology matters because several of these are highly chemosensitive.

Not every SVCO is malignant. An **aortic or innominate aneurysm** can mimic a malignant mediastinal mass, with stridor and hoarseness, and a very large **retrosternal goitre** can block the SVC while also causing stridor and dysphagia.

Typical picture: **swollen face and arms**, **distended neck and arm veins**, and a **dusky colour** over the face, arms and chest. Dilated **collateral veins** appear on the chest wall over weeks, and seeing blood flow through them supports the diagnosis. Back-pressure can cause **headache** that is worse on bending forward, stooping or lying down.

blocks.title: Other features described
items: **Subconjunctival/conjunctival oedema**, with oedema and cyanosis of the head, neck, hands and arms.
Breathlessness and/or difficulty swallowing, and sometimes **stridor**.
Quick-source triad in lung cancer: facial swelling, breathlessness, distended veins of the neck and upper chest.
Engorged **supraclavicular** veins with facial swelling.
On respiratory examination, prominent chest wall veins should make you think of SVCO.

blocks.text: The **JVP is raised but non-pulsatile** in SVCO. Compare malignant pericardial effusion, where the JVP rises with tachycardia, falling blood pressure, muffled heart sounds and Kussmaul’s sign.

**Pemberton’s sign**: raising both arms above the head brings on facial congestion and cyanosis. Zero to Finals uses it for SVCO; Davidson includes it in the thyroid examination, and a very large retrosternal goitre is itself a cause of SVCO.

Frequencies differ between books. Pocket Medicine gives face/arm swelling in >80%, neck/chest vein distension ~60%, breathlessness/cough ~50% and headache ~10%. Follow **Davidson**: **dyspnoea (63%)** is the commonest symptom and **neck vein distension (66%)** the commonest sign.

Pocket Medicine lists SVC syndrome in the differential of a raised JVP with Kussmaul’s sign (alongside constrictive pericarditis and tricuspid stenosis). Davidson stresses the distinguishing point: in SVCO the raised JVP **does not pulsate**.

blocks.note: Look at: the clinical photo of SVC obstruction in a patient with a mediastinal mass (facial swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins).
Look at: prominent jugular venous distension in SVC syndrome caused by a central malignant lesion.

blocks.title: Core work-up
items: **CT thorax (contrast-enhanced)** is the investigation of choice. It confirms SVCO, shows the level of obstruction and separates **extrinsic compression** from **intraluminal thrombus**.
**Tissue diagnosis** when the tumour type is unknown: histology largely decides between chemotherapy, radiotherapy and stenting.
**CT head** if cerebral oedema is suspected (postural headache, confusion).

blocks.title: Ways to get tissue from a mediastinal mass
rows: Often needed to obtain histology; may remove part or all of the tumour
Needle aspirate of an enlarged supraclavicular node
Simple cytological diagnosis in suspected lung cancer

blocks.text: On a **chest X-ray**, a malignant mediastinal tumour usually has a **poorly defined edge** and looks like general widening of the mediastinum, whereas a benign one tends to be **sharply circumscribed**. CT (or MRI) is the imaging of choice for mediastinal masses.

blocks.note: Look at: the four mediastinal compartments and where common tumours sit (lymphoid masses, thymus, teratoma/dermoid, retrosternal thyroid, neurogenic tumours).

blocks.text: In a **stable** patient, do not give radiotherapy before histology is obtained: upfront radiotherapy can obscure the pathological diagnosis, and the wrong tumour type means the wrong treatment.

blocks.title: Life-threatening complications
items: **Cerebral oedema** from venous back-pressure: headache worse on stooping or lying flat, then confusion or stupor; it can progress to cerebral ischaemia and herniation.
**Laryngeal / upper-airway oedema**: stridor and life-threatening airway narrowing.
Some patients need **ventilatory support** until treatment relieves the obstruction. Decide early, based on the likely prognosis.

blocks.title: The same mediastinal mass can hit neighbouring structures

blocks.text: Bedside red flags in SVCO: **stridor, headache and confusion**. Stridor or stupor means emergency treatment (stent and/or radiotherapy) rather than waiting for histology.
Long-term outcome is set mainly by the **underlying cancer**. Relieving the SVCO should be followed by treatment of the primary tumour where possible.

Davidson’s sequence: **confirm with CT → get histology if unknown → relieve the obstruction with chemotherapy, radiotherapy or a stent according to tumour type → treat the primary**. Patients with stridor or reduced consciousness need emergency relief first.

blocks.title: Choosing treatment
rows: Highly chemosensitive tumour (lymphoma, germ-cell tumour; SCLC in Kumar and Washington)
Masses are often large and the disease more widespread, so systemic treatment is preferred
Relatively chemo-/radio-resistant tumours (NSCLC, carcinoma of unknown primary)
Rapid effect and can be repeated; increasingly favoured over radiotherapy

blocks.title: Steroids — the books disagree
items: **Kumar & Clark** (and K&C Essentials): immediate steroids, chemotherapy if the tumour should respond, possibly mediastinal radiotherapy; stents and anticoagulation sometimes needed.
**Pocket Medicine**: steroids, diuretics, radiotherapy ± chemotherapy; stent if severe; anticoagulate if clot.

**Washington Manual**: steroids have a role in steroid-responsive tumours (**lymphoma, thymoma**); for other cancers their role is unclear and they are not recommended; use for airway oedema is only anecdotal.
**Davidson**: the SVCO section does not mention steroids at all.

blocks.text: Do not answer “steroids for everyone”. Davidson’s plan is histology first, then chemotherapy, radiotherapy or stenting. If a question asks where steroids clearly help, the defensible answer is a steroid-responsive tumour such as **lymphoma**.

NSCLC: Washington’s emergency table pairs it with radiotherapy, but Davidson notes that **stenting is increasingly favoured** for relatively chemo-/radio-resistant tumours such as NSCLC because it is rapid and repeatable. Follow Davidson.
In lung cancer, palliative radiotherapy is most useful for distressing local problems: **SVCO**, recurrent haemoptysis, chest wall or bone pain, and airway obstruction.

cards.back: Extrinsic compression (or invasion) by a mass, and intraluminal blockage (thrombus, e.g. catheter-related or tumour-associated).

cards.front: What decides how severe and how sudden SVCO symptoms are?
cards.back: The speed of occlusion versus how well venous collaterals have developed.
Lung cancer (via malignant mediastinal nodes); lymphoma is the other major malignant cause.

cards.front: Which leukaemia characteristically causes a mediastinal mass with SVCO?
Two benign compressive causes of SVCO in Davidson?
cards.back: Large retrosternal goitre and thoracic aortic aneurysm.

cards.front: Commonest symptom and sign of SVCO (Davidson Box 33.12)?

cards.back: Facial congestion and cyanosis when both arms are raised above the head (SVCO, retrosternal goitre).
Contrast-enhanced CT thorax: confirms the obstruction, shows its level and separates extrinsic from intraluminal causes.

cards.front: Why get a biopsy before treating SVCO of unknown cause?
cards.back: Tumour type largely decides treatment; upfront radiotherapy in a stable patient can obscure the histology.

cards.front: SVCO patient with headache worse on stooping and new confusion: what complication and what test?
cards.back: Cerebral oedema from venous back-pressure; CT head.

cards.front: Cause of stridor as an SVCO complication, and its urgent treatment?
cards.back: Laryngeal/upper-airway oedema; emergency stent and/or radiotherapy.

cards.front: SVCO tumours that may need chemotherapy alone?
cards.back: Highly chemosensitive ones: lymphoma and germ-cell tumours (plus SCLC in Kumar and Washington).

cards.front: Response to mediastinal radiotherapy in SVCO?
cards.back: Symptom relief within 2 weeks in 50–90% of patients.

cards.front: Why is SVC stenting increasingly favoured?
cards.back: It works quickly and can be repeated; especially useful for NSCLC or carcinoma of unknown primary.

cards.front: When is anticoagulation indicated in SVCO?
cards.back: When thrombus is present in the SVC.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has had a tunnelled central venous catheter for chemotherapy for four months. Over three days her face and right arm swell and she notices distended veins over her upper chest. Contrast CT shows no mediastinal mass.
questions.leadIn: Which mechanism best explains her superior vena cava obstruction?
options: Extrinsic compression by mediastinal lymph nodes
Intraluminal thrombosis related to the catheter
Raised right atrial pressure from a pericardial effusion
Obstruction of the inferior vena cava
Direct tumour invasion through the SVC wall
questions.explanation: SVCO arises either from outside pressure on the vein or from blockage inside it. With a long-term central line and **no mass on CT**, the likely cause is **catheter-related thrombosis**, one of the intravascular causes Davidson lists.
whyNot: No mass was seen on CT, so nodal compression is unlikely.
A pericardial effusion raises a pulsatile JVP with hypotension and muffled heart sounds; it does not cause localised upper-body venous obstruction.
IVC compression causes leg oedema, not facial and arm swelling.
Invasion needs a tumour next to the SVC, and none was seen.

questions.stem: Two patients have SVCO from the same type of tumour. Patient A developed severe facial swelling and breathlessness over 48 hours. Patient B has had mild facial fullness developing over two months and has prominent dilated veins across the chest wall.
questions.leadIn: What best explains why patient B has milder symptoms?
options: Venous collaterals have had time to develop
questions.explanation: Symptom severity depends on **how quickly** the SVC closes and on the **collateral circulation**. Slow occlusion over weeks lets collaterals open (the visible chest wall veins), which softens the picture.
whyNot: Tumour size alone does not explain it; the timescale and collaterals do.
SVCO is a venous outflow problem above the heart; right atrial pressure is not the issue.
Nothing suggests steroid treatment, and it would not explain the chest wall veins.
Either mechanism can be slow or fast; the dilated collaterals point to time, not mechanism.

questions.theme: Causes of superior vena cava obstruction
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Bronchial carcinoma with mediastinal nodal spread

items.stem: A 66-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years has had haemoptysis and weight loss for two months. He now has a puffy face and dilated veins over his upper chest. CT shows a right hilar mass with bulky paratracheal nodes pressing on the SVC.
items.explanation: Lung cancer is the commonest cause of SVCO, typically through malignant mediastinal nodes compressing the vein. The smoking history, haemoptysis and hilar mass make it clear.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman with intestinal failure receives home parenteral nutrition through a long-term central line. Both arms and her face become swollen. Contrast CT shows a filling defect inside the SVC and no mediastinal mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: parenteral nutrition means a long-term central line, and a filling defect without a mass means intraluminal clot. Line thrombosis is often seen on imaging, but clinical SVC syndrome from it is uncommon.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had a slowly growing neck swelling for 20 years. She now has noisy breathing, difficulty swallowing solids, and her face becomes congested when she lifts her arms above her head.
items.explanation: A long-standing neck swelling extending into the chest, with stridor and dysphagia, is a large retrosternal goitre. A positive Pemberton’s sign fits, and Davidson notes that such goitres can obstruct the SVC.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with known lung cancer is admitted with suspected SVCO.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson’s frequency data, which symptom is reported most often in SVCO?
questions.explanation: Box 33.12 lists **dyspnoea in 63%**, ahead of facial swelling/head fullness (50%), cough (24%), arm swelling (18%), chest pain (15%) and dysphagia (9%). Other books give different figures; follow Davidson.
whyNot: Least common in the list (9%).
Only about 15%.
About 18%.
Common (50%) but second to dyspnoea in Davidson; Pocket Medicine ranks swelling higher.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with a mediastinal mass has facial oedema and plethora. Her neck veins are distended to the angle of the jaw while she sits upright.
questions.leadIn: Which finding on inspecting the jugular venous pulse is most typical of SVCO?
options: Raised with a prominent y descent that rises on inspiration
Normal height with cannon a waves
questions.explanation: In SVCO the venous column is cut off from the right heart, so the JVP is **elevated but non-pulsatile**. A pulsatile raised JVP points instead to a cardiac or pericardial cause.
whyNot: Typical of constrictive pericarditis (Kussmaul’s sign), which Pocket Medicine lists in the same differential.
Giant v waves suggest tricuspid regurgitation, a pulsatile cardiac sign.
Cannon waves come from atrioventricular dissociation, not venous obstruction.
A low JVP suggests hypovolaemia, the opposite of SVCO.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Ultrasound-guided needle aspirate of a supraclavicular node

items.stem: A 57-year-old smoker has had facial swelling and distended neck veins for 10 days. The team wants one test that confirms the obstruction, shows its level and shows whether it is caused by an external mass or by clot in the vein.
items.explanation: Contrast CT thorax is the investigation of choice. It confirms SVCO and separates extravascular from intravascular causes.

items.stem: A man with confirmed SVCO from a mediastinal mass develops a headache that is worse whenever he lies flat or bends forward, and he has become drowsy.
items.explanation: A postural headache with drowsiness suggests cerebral oedema from venous back-pressure. Davidson advises CT of the head when this is suspected.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman has SVCO from a mediastinal mass of unknown type. A hard 2-cm lump is felt just above her left clavicle.
items.explanation: Histology is needed before treatment. An enlarged supraclavicular node gives the simplest route to a cytological diagnosis, avoiding more invasive mediastinal sampling.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with SVCO from lymphoma describes a severe headache that is worse when he stoops or lies down. Today he is newly confused.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause of his headache?
options: Cerebral oedema from raised venous back-pressure
questions.explanation: Blocked venous drainage from the head causes **cerebral oedema**. The headache typically worsens on stooping or lying flat, and confusion is a danger sign that can precede herniation.
whyNot: Possible in cancer, but the postural pattern tied to SVCO points to venous back-pressure; CT head would distinguish them.
No fever or meningism is described.
Causes confusion but not a postural headache.
Presents with a sudden thunderclap headache, not a postural one.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with SVCO from a mediastinal mass develops inspiratory stridor over a few hours, with marked swelling of the face and neck.
questions.leadIn: Which complication is the stridor most likely to represent?
questions.explanation: Venous outflow obstruction can cause **laryngeal and upper-airway oedema**, a life-threatening complication that needs emergency stenting and/or radiotherapy.
whyNot: Causes hoarseness and a bovine cough rather than acute stridor.
Causes a paralysed hemidiaphragm, not stridor.
Causes expiratory wheeze, not inspiratory stridor with facial swelling.
Causes breathlessness with tracheal deviation and hypotension, not stridor.

questions.theme: Treatment of SVCO by clinical scenario
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 23-year-old man has SVCO from a large anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows a germ-cell tumour.
items.explanation: Germ-cell tumours (like lymphoma) are highly chemosensitive, so Davidson allows chemotherapy alone.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man has SVCO from biopsy-proven non-small-cell lung cancer. He is distressed by facial swelling and needs relief within days. His tumour is expected to respond poorly to chemotherapy.
items.explanation: Stenting gives rapid, repeatable relief and is particularly useful for relatively chemo- and radio-resistant tumours such as NSCLC.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long-term central line develops SVCO. CT shows thrombus within the SVC and no mass.
items.explanation: With SVC thrombosis and no tumour, anticoagulation is indicated.

questions.theme: Local effects of a malignant mediastinal mass
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus

items.stem: A 64-year-old smoker with a left hilar mass has a weak, breathy voice and a cough that has lost its normal explosive quality.
items.explanation: Paralysis of the left vocal cord gives hoarseness and a “bovine” cough, from involvement of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

items.stem: A 59-year-old woman with a mediastinal mass has new breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a raised right hemidiaphragm, and screening confirms it is paralysed.
items.explanation: Phrenic nerve involvement paralyses the hemidiaphragm on that side.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has non-pulsatile distended neck veins, subconjunctival oedema and dilated veins across the chest wall.
items.explanation: These are Davidson’s signs of SVC obstruction by a mediastinal mass. The non-pulsatile JVP is the key clue.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with a mediastinal tumour has a drooping left eyelid and a small left pupil. He has no arm pain and no hand weakness.
items.explanation: Ptosis and miosis are Horner’s syndrome from sympathetic trunk involvement. The lack of arm symptoms argues against brachial plexus invasion.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has facial swelling, distended neck veins and dusky skin over the upper chest. Chest X-ray shows a widened upper mediastinum.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation should be done next to confirm SVCO and define its cause?
questions.explanation: CT thorax is the investigation of choice. It confirms the obstruction, shows its level, and separates extrinsic compression from thrombus.
whyNot: Useful for pericardial effusion, but it cannot show the SVC and mediastinum.
Looks at the wrong venous territory.
Can sample tissue later, but it does not confirm SVCO or show its cause.
Only needed for suspected cerebral oedema (and CT head is the test Davidson suggests).

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with SVCO from squamous cell lung cancer starts mediastinal radiotherapy. He asks how likely it is to help and how soon.
questions.leadIn: Which statement best matches Davidson’s figure?
options: Symptoms improve within 2 weeks in about 50–90%
Symptoms improve within 24 hours in almost all
Symptoms improve within 2 weeks in under 10%
No benefit is expected for 3 months
Benefit only follows a full course of chemotherapy
questions.explanation: Mediastinal radiotherapy relieves SVCO symptoms within **2 weeks in 50–90%** of patients. When faster relief is needed, stenting works more quickly.
whyNot: Too fast; rapid relief is the advantage of stenting, not radiotherapy.
Far too pessimistic.
Wrong timescale.
Radiotherapy works on its own in tumours that are not chemosensitive.

questions.stem: During examination of a woman with suspected SVCO, she is asked to lift both arms above her head. Within a minute her face becomes congested and cyanosed.
questions.leadIn: What is this bedside sign called?
questions.explanation: Facial congestion with the arms raised is **Pemberton’s sign**, seen with SVC obstruction and with retrosternal goitre.
whyNot: A paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration (constriction, effusion).
Carpal spasm with a cuff, seen in hypocalcaemia.
Facial twitch on tapping the facial nerve, seen in hypocalcaemia.
Calf pain on dorsiflexion, an outdated DVT sign.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had facial swelling and dilated chest wall veins for three weeks. CT confirms extrinsic compression of the SVC by a mediastinal mass. Histology is awaited.
questions.leadIn: Which underlying malignancy is statistically most likely?
questions.explanation: **Lung cancer** is the most common cause of SVCO, usually through malignant mediastinal nodes. Lymphoma and metastatic tumours are the other main malignant causes.
whyNot: A major cause, but lung cancer is the most common.
Metastatic tumours can do it, but less often than lung cancer.
A recognised cause, but much less frequent than lung cancer.
A recognised cause, but much less frequent than lung cancer.

questions.theme: Raised venous pressure and facial swelling in a patient with cancer
questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Acute cor pulmonale from pulmonary embolism

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with lung cancer has a puffy face and swollen arms. His neck veins are distended but no pulsation can be seen. Dilated veins run across his chest wall. Blood pressure and heart sounds are normal.
items.explanation: Step 1: the swelling is limited to the upper body, so think of venous obstruction rather than a systemic cause. Step 2: the JVP is raised but **non-pulsatile**, which places the problem above the heart. Step 3: chest wall collaterals confirm a slowly developing obstruction, so this is SVCO.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with breast cancer becomes breathless. Her pulse is 118/min, her blood pressure has fallen from 120/80 to 88/60 over a few hours, her JVP is rising and her heart sounds are muffled.
items.explanation: Step 1: raised JVP with **hypotension and tachycardia** means the heart cannot fill. Step 2: muffled heart sounds suggest fluid around the heart. Step 3: in a patient with cancer, a malignant pericardial effusion fits; Davidson lists these signs in the cancer examination.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has ascites and leg oedema. His JVP is raised, with a prominent y descent, and it rises further on inspiration. He is not tachycardic and has no pulsus paradoxus.
items.explanation: Step 1: a **pulsatile** raised JVP rules out SVCO. Step 2: a prominent y descent plus Kussmaul’s sign without pulsus paradoxus is the pattern of constriction. Step 3: no hypotension or tachycardia makes acute tamponade unlikely, so constrictive pericarditis fits best.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has had facial swelling for three weeks. She is comfortable at rest, alert, and has no stridor. Contrast CT shows a 7-cm anterior mediastinal mass compressing the SVC. She has no previous cancer diagnosis. The on-call registrar suggests starting mediastinal radiotherapy tonight.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Obtain tissue for histology before tumour-directed treatment
questions.explanation: Step 1: is she in danger? No stridor and no confusion, so she is **stable** and there is time. Step 2: the tumour type is unknown, and that largely decides between chemotherapy (lymphoma, germ-cell), radiotherapy and stenting. Step 3: radiotherapy before biopsy can obscure the pathology, so **get tissue first**; mediastinoscopy suits an anterior mass.
whyNot: In a stable patient, upfront radiotherapy risks obscuring the histology.
Emergency stenting is for stridor or reduced consciousness; she has neither.
Treatment depends on tumour type, so empirical chemotherapy could be wrong.
CT shows extrinsic compression by a mass, not thrombus.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.
options: Raised intracranial pressure from brain metastases

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with small-cell lung cancer has had a headache for a week that is worst when she bends to tie her shoes. Her face looks puffy each morning and there are distended veins across her upper chest.
items.explanation: A postural headache might suggest raised intracranial pressure, but facial swelling and distended upper chest veins show the cause is venous back-pressure from SVCO.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man with bulky high-grade lymphoma has palpitations two days after his first chemotherapy. Potassium, phosphate and urate are high and calcium is low.
items.explanation: Massive tumour breakdown after treatment releases potassium, phosphate and urate, with secondary hypocalcaemia: tumour lysis syndrome.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has had back pain for weeks. Since yesterday both legs feel weak.
items.explanation: New leg weakness in a cancer patient is spinal cord compression until proved otherwise; whole-spine MRI is the test.

items.stem: Ten days after chemotherapy, a 45-year-old woman has a temperature of 38°C lasting more than an hour. Her neutrophil count is 0.3 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: A temperature of 38°C for more than an hour with neutrophils below 0.5 × 10⁹/L meets Davidson’s definition of neutropenic fever, an emergency.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 64-year-old man with SVCO from known NSCLC develops stridor and becomes stuporous over a few hours.
items.explanation: Stridor (laryngeal oedema) or stupor (cerebral oedema) needs emergency relief with a stent and/or radiotherapy. Stenting works rapidly and suits relatively resistant NSCLC.

items.stem: A 58-year-old stable woman has SVCO. Biopsy of the mediastinal mass shows small-cell lung cancer.
items.explanation: SCLC is chemosensitive. Kumar and Washington both make chemotherapy the treatment of choice, and the disease is often already widespread.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man’s SVCO from carcinoma of unknown primary was relieved by a stent last week. He asks what will most influence his long-term outcome.
items.explanation: Davidson: relieving SVCO should be followed by treatment of the primary where possible, because long-term outcome depends on the underlying cancer.

questions.stem: Five patients each have SVCO from a biopsy-proven mediastinal tumour.
questions.leadIn: In which tumour is chemotherapy alone most likely to be the appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Highly chemosensitive tumours such as **lymphoma** and germ-cell tumours can be treated with chemotherapy alone. Most other tumours need radiotherapy or stenting.
whyNot: Relatively chemo-resistant; Davidson favours stenting (or radiotherapy).
Relatively resistant; stenting is particularly useful here.
Not chemosensitive enough for chemotherapy alone.
Washington pairs thymic tumours with surgery, not chemotherapy alone.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has had slowly increasing facial fullness for six weeks. Several tortuous, dilated veins now run across the front of his chest.
questions.leadIn: What do these chest wall veins most likely represent?
options: Collateral channels around a superior vena cava obstruction
questions.explanation: Collaterals develop over **weeks** around an obstructed SVC, and blood flow through them helps confirm the diagnosis. Facial fullness fits upper-body venous obstruction.
whyNot: Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus with signs of liver disease, not facial swelling.
Gives a tender, red cord, not widespread dilated veins with facial swelling.
Causes small mucocutaneous telangiectases and bleeding, not large collaterals.
Small arteriolar lesions, not tortuous venous channels.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy has had two weeks of tiredness and bruising. He now has facial swelling and distended neck veins. White cell count is 85 × 10⁹/L with many blasts. Chest X-ray shows a mediastinal mass.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A mediastinal mass causing SVCO is the characteristic feature of **ALL** in Kumar’s leukaemia table. Kumar’s Fig. 6.17 shows the same picture in T-lymphoblastic disease.
whyNot: Acute leukaemia with blasts, but a mediastinal mass is a feature of ALL, not AML.
A disease of older adults, without blasts or a mediastinal mass.
A chronic leukaemia with a raised white count of mature cells and splenomegaly, not a mediastinal mass.
Rare in teenagers; causes pancytopenia and splenomegaly.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 25-year-old man has a well-defined mass in the posterior mediastinum found on a routine chest X-ray. He has no symptoms.
items.explanation: Neurogenic tumours sit in the posterior mediastinum (Davidson Fig. 17.52).

items.stem: A 74-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has hoarseness, stridor and early SVCO from a superior mediastinal “mass”. CT angiography shows the mass fills with contrast in continuity with the aortic arch.
items.explanation: Two steps: a mass that fills with contrast continuous with the aorta is vascular, not neoplastic. Thoracic aneurysms cause compressive features, including SVC syndrome, and mimic malignant mediastinal tumours.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a sharply circumscribed anterior mediastinal mass. Months later the lesion ruptures into a bronchus and she coughs up its contents.
items.explanation: Benign mediastinal tumours are well defined; Davidson notes that a dermoid cyst may occasionally rupture into a bronchus.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with SVCO has a chest X-ray showing poorly defined, general broadening of the upper mediastinum.
questions.leadIn: What does this appearance most suggest?
questions.explanation: A malignant mediastinal tumour seldom has a clear margin and usually shows as **general mediastinal widening**. Benign masses tend to be sharply circumscribed. CT is the next step.
whyNot: Benign masses are usually sharply outlined.
Usually a well-defined rounded opacity.
Benign, well defined, and posterior.
Would not explain SVCO in a 60-year-old.

questions.leadIn: Pick the single best match from the list for each patient below. Any option can be the answer for several patients, or for none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man has two weeks of increasing breathlessness and facial swelling. CT shows a bulky anterior mediastinal mass. Biopsy shows immature lymphoid blasts of T-cell lineage.
items.explanation: This matches Kumar’s example of a bulky anterior mediastinal mass in T-lymphoblastic lymphoma presenting with SVCO.

items.stem: A 67-year-old smoker is found to have a sodium of 121 mmol/L with inappropriately concentrated urine. A week later he develops facial swelling and dilated veins on his chest. CT shows a central lung mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: hyponatraemia from SIADH points to small-cell lung cancer, and a central lung tumour compressing the SVC causes SVCO. Step-Up notes SVCO is more common with SCLC.

items.stem: An 80-year-old woman has known thyroid enlargement for decades. CT shows a mass continuous with the thyroid that extends behind the sternum and narrows both the trachea and the SVC.
items.explanation: A very large goitre extending into the mediastinum can cause stridor, dysphagia and SVC obstruction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has SVCO. While definitive treatment is being planned, the team debates adding corticosteroids. The books disagree on their role.
questions.leadIn: In which underlying tumour do corticosteroids have the clearest role?
questions.explanation: Washington gives steroids a role in **steroid-responsive tumours such as lymphoma and thymoma** and does not recommend them for other cancers. Kumar & Clark give immediate steroids more broadly, while Davidson’s SVCO section omits them. The safe exam answer is lymphoma.
whyNot: Not steroid-responsive; stenting or radiotherapy relieve SVCO here.
Not steroid-responsive, and a rare cause of SVCO.
Not steroid-responsive.
No evidence of steroid response; stenting is particularly useful.

ospe.identify: Clinical photo: superior vena cava obstruction in a patient with a mediastinal mass. Look for facial swelling and distended neck and chest wall veins.
Prominent jugular venous distension: SVC syndrome caused by a central malignant lesion obstructing the SVC.
Bulky anterior mediastinal mass (T-lymphoblastic lymphoma) causing superior vena caval obstruction.
Mediastinal compartments with typical tumour sites: lymphoid masses, thymus, teratoma/dermoid, retrosternal thyroid, and neurogenic tumours posteriorly.
